analysis.one_liner: Requires written notice and a waiting period before a person with a disability can sue a business over an inaccessible building.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 225-192 on February 15, 2018, almost entirely on party lines, but the Senate never voted and it died when the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would keep a person with a disability from filing a federal lawsuit over a blocked entrance, missing ramp, or other physical barrier until they first sent the business a detailed written notice and waited: 60 days for the owner to respond with a written improvement plan, then up to 60 more days to remove the barrier or make "substantial progress." It also directs the Justice Department to run an education program for property owners and sets up a mediation program as an alternative to court. The stated goal is to stop abusive demand letters against small businesses; the practical effect is that the main federal tool for forcing stores and restaurants to become accessible — a lawsuit — becomes slow, procedural, and easier for owners to stall.
analysis.who_benefits: Owners and operators of stores, restaurants, hotels, and other public accommodations, especially those facing demand letters or suits over accessibility violations, gain a shield: nothing can go to court until months of notice and response have passed, and a written promise of future work can buy more time. National chains and commercial landlords, which face the most ADA suits, gain the most from the delay.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Business owners and landlords facing ADA lawsuits

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits a civil action over an architectural barrier unless the person first gave the owner written notice identifying the barrier and the circumstances of the denial [S3][S4][S5].

Gives the owner 60 days to reply with a written description of planned improvements, and if the removal takes longer, 60 more days to remove the barrier or make substantial progress before anyone may sue [S5].
Directs the Justice Department to educate state and local governments and property owners on strategies for making public accommodations accessible, using existing funding only [S2][S5].
Directs the federal courts' policy body to create a model mediation program so claims are resolved before costly litigation [S3][S5].

analysis.who_pays: People with disabilities bear the cost if the bill passes: they lose the ability to go straight to federal court when a business is inaccessible, must document and describe each denial in writing, and must wait out cure periods while the inaccessible door or counter stays as it is. The remedy shifts from enforcing a civil right to negotiating with the party that violated it.
analysis.who_pays_short: People with disabilities denied accessible access

drawbacks.text: A person denied entry must write a detailed notice — the address, the circumstances of the denial, whether the barrier was permanent — then wait 60 days, and if the owner promises fixes in writing, wait up to 60 more while the business remains inaccessible [S5].
The education program is funded only "based on existing funding" at the Justice Department, so the affirmative-help half of the bill has no new money attached [S5].

The strongest good-faith argument for it: some law firms have sent hundreds of identical demand letters to small businesses over minor technical violations, and a notice-and-cure step gives owners a chance to fix problems without paying a settlement. But the bill does not distinguish a real blocked door from a technical footfault — both now require months of notice before court.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The mediation and education provisions are sensible on their face, but the bill's core is a procedural wall in front of a civil right, and the wall's cost falls entirely on the people the ADA was written to protect. A narrower bill targeting abusive demand letters — without a 60- to 120-day toll for every genuine access denial — would have answered the stated problem without making accessibility enforcement dependent on the violator's cooperation.

outcome.mechanism: It passed the House 225-192 in February 2018, was received by the Senate nine days later, and the Senate never brought it to a vote before the Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: The House Judiciary Committee ordered the bill reported on a 15-9 vote in September 2017 and reported it in January 2018 [S7].
The House passed it on February 15, 2018, 225-192: 213 of 237 voting Republicans in favor, 173 of 193 voting Democrats against [S8].
The Senate received the bill on February 26, 2018, and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress [S7].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People with disabilities kept immediate access to federal court over inaccessible businesses. Businesses hoping for relief from ADA demand letters gained nothing; the House-passed language simply expired.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: People with disabilities, whose right to sue survived

for.name: Ted Poe
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and sponsored a floor amendment during House consideration [S1][S7].

for.name: Bob Goodlatte
for.what_they_did: Steered the bill through committee markup (reported 15-9) and moved its passage on the House floor [S7].

for.name: Retail, restaurant, hotel, and business trade groups
for.what_they_did: Publicly backed the bill as relief from serial ADA lawsuits.

against.name: Jim Langevin
against.role: U.S. Representative (D-RI), wheelchair user and disability-rights advocate
against.what_they_did: Offered a floor amendment during House consideration and voted against passage [S7][S8].

against.name: Disability rights organizations
against.role: National disability advocacy groups (e.g., the National Federation of the Blind and the Consortium for Citizens with Disabilities)
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill, arguing the notice-and-cure period strips the enforcement tool behind ADA access without fixing the actual barrier problem.

sides.party_line_note: The floor vote split sharply by party — 213 of 237 voting Republicans in favor, 173 of 193 voting Democrats against — though 12 Democrats and 19 Republicans crossed lines [S8].

industries.industry: Retailers, restaurants, hotels, and other public accommodations
industries.note: The bill would make it impossible to sue these businesses over a physical access barrier until months of notice and response have passed, and a written promise of future work buys more time. Their gain — litigation delay — is disabled customers' continued exclusion from inaccessible premises.
Owners facing ADA claims gain a mandatory cure period and a slower path to liability, while the burden of documenting and waiting shifts to the disabled person denied access.

Firms that bring ADA access suits would face a notice-and-cure requirement that removes their quick-filing leverage; the suits they bring are the mechanism the ADA relies on to open businesses to disabled customers.
